The argument also implies that the nature would turn into existence. — س ره

If the relation to the maker were an ordinary relation between things, it could not make “existent” truly apply, because such a relation is only a mental consideration. Before it is made, a nature considered in itself and apart from its relation to its maker is also only a mental consideration. Adding one mental consideration to another cannot establish reality. But if the relation is an illuminating relation, it is real existence itself. Existence is then primary in making and reality, and nature is an idea drawn from it, as the sound view holds. — س ره

The author says “some” to exclude natures defined by their relation to something else. He uses “maker” as a hidden example within the broad class of “other things,” including existence, which is closer to a nature than anything else and cannot be separated from it even in thought. It is as if he said that we can think of a nature without thinking of its existence, its being made existent, or its maker. A particular existence, however, depends on all-pervading existence—the maker’s light, presence, and active support. In one respect, the relation of particular existences to this all-pervading existence is like the relation of a nature’s essential parts to the nature. — س ره

This does not mean that a nature is universal in itself. It means that its own nature allows the mind to consider it as universal. If it were already particular in itself, it could not be considered universal. — س ره

One might ask: if existence is an idea drawn by the mind, how can it make something particular? The answer is that some say particularity is part of how the mind analyses a nature. A thing’s particular identity is its own “thisness,” not something added to it. It becomes particular through its existence, and its existence through its relation to its maker. — س ره

The general nature, whether considered as one individual or as one of many possible instances, has the same relation to its maker. The maker must therefore determine it as one particular thing before bringing it about. This applies when a nature has only one possible instance. Otherwise, its particularity must also depend on differences in matter and readiness. — ن ره

The commentator takes the question to mean that the maker causes the thing’s particularity. He does not consider another possible meaning: that the thing becomes particular through its relation to the maker, as some mystics hold. But the maker’s relation to itself cannot make something else particular. The author’s point can also be read this way: a thing can be particular through its maker only if existence is what is made, since existence depends on its maker while a nature can be considered apart from it. — س ره

A nature’s necessary result follows from existence, since, in the view of these thinkers, God has no nature apart from existence. A necessary feature of a nature is only a mental idea, because it follows from the nature when we consider it apart from its necessity and its maker. The nature, considered in this way, is itself only an idea. — س ره

Suhrawardi says that light is one reality, though some instances exist by themselves and others belong to a subject. Why could existence not work the same way, with some instances—God, the intelligences, and souls—existing by themselves, while others belong to a nature? This seems the best way to understand him. His earlier arguments show that existence cannot be an outside feature added to a nature; they do not show that one instance of a single reality cannot exist by itself while another depends on something else. Nor do they show that existence cannot belong to one nature when it cannot belong to that same nature considered in itself. — س ره
Being real is part of what existence is, so it cannot become merely mental. — س ره

The point is to show that existence is what is made, and that natures are not. The first argument was that what is made directly must itself be a relation of dependence. This is true of particular existence. It also shows that made things cannot be mere necessary features of natures, since such features remain even when we ignore their maker. But if what is made is existence, it is itself a relation and cannot be separated from its maker. The second argument is that, if everything except the first made thing were a necessary feature of a nature, it would be only a mental idea. The author’s aim is to show that the maker’s effects are not such features. — س ره

Since real bringing-about is existence related to God, and true making is existence, the two descriptions point to the same thing. “Equal” here means that neither existence nor nonexistence is prior. Those who allow priority explain possibility as the possibility of either side. The definition by denying necessity, as used in logic, is more exact. However one defines it, this possibility does not apply to particular existence. — س ره
A nature can be conceived apart from its existence, which in one sense is its own being, let alone apart from its being made or from its maker. It is empty of everything but itself. — س ره

If what is made is existence, what do you think the maker must be? If even existence in general is the basis of causation, then all the more is this true of pure existence—the Necessary Being, beyond every limit of completeness. He alone is the true maker, as the author says. — س ره
The source appears to mean “the Second Teacher,” al-Farabi. A copyist may have changed the wording. — س ره
Some copies read “compound predication” here instead of “compound statement.”
Some copies read “the compound existential predication” here.

For this thinker, what is made is the existent thing, not existence itself, since he recognizes no individual instance of existence, either in the mind or outside it. His view comes close to the truth. It differs from that of his contemporary, the scholar al-Dawani: al-Dawani says that a nature is made simply as that nature, while this thinker says it is made insofar as it exists. — س ره

If he means that people do not say this in ordinary speech, that settles nothing; philosophical truths are not decided by common usage. If he means that no one says blackness comes from an agent through a compound act of making, who would deny that? But that does not prove his point. If he means that reason does not say blackness comes from an agent through simple making—that blackness itself issues from the agent—then that is false. Many thinkers have held this view. — س ره

Every passage quoted from Bahmanyar shows how deeply he understood these questions, how sound his reasoning was, and how thoroughly he had studied philosophy. The student reflects the teacher; like master, like pupil. — س ره

Perhaps the author thought Bahmanyar meant that composite natures are made while simple natures are not. Al-Tusi seems to make this point in The Abstract of Belief: “Just as a composite needs a maker, so does a simple thing.” The author may be clarifying what Bahmanyar meant. — س ره
That is, natures help explain why existences differ, while existences are what make the differences real. So there is no circular argument. — س ره

One might object: if each nature is an independent cause, two independent causes would converge on one effect; if the group of them is the cause, then the differences would not belong to the natures themselves. The author points to two ways of explaining the differences. On the first, because natures are ideas, their differences in reality follow from differences among existences, and the differences among existences belong to them in themselves. In that case, “substance is substance by itself” refers to existent substance, and “accident is accident by itself” to existent accident. On the second account, the differences among existences as known by the mind follow from differences among natures, and those differences belong to the natures themselves. Here, “substance is substance by itself” refers to the nature of substance, and “accident is accident by itself” to the nature of accident. A further account says that the natures in this world reflect differences in earlier forms and realms of knowledge, and that those earlier differences reflect the meanings of God’s names and attributes. Those meanings are unmade without God’s essence being unmade. One may also understand “substance is substance by itself” to mean that a thing’s being itself is necessary and needs no cause. This denies compound making, not simple making, as Bahmanyar’s words already suggest. — س ره
This means restricting or conditioning the act of making, whether by what is best, by the time of the act, or by some other limit proposed by those who say the flow of existence can stop. — س ره
His manifestation is His appearance. The appearance of a thing cannot be separate from it; otherwise it would not be that thing’s appearance. — س ره

This is drawn from a saying of the leader of the saints and guide of the pure, Ali. Asked about the higher world, he said: “Forms without matter, free of potentiality and readiness: He appeared to them, and they shone; He looked upon them, and they gleamed; He cast His image into their reality and brought His acts forth through them.” — س ره
This phrase belongs with what comes before “be careful”; it is unrelated to what follows. — س ره

The author relies on observation because most of his arguments follow the path of studying natures. In philosophical questions like this, someone who follows the path of existence has more room to argue. Existence is a real reality with different levels of strength and weakness. A weaker existence depends on and is constituted by a stronger one. This is possible only if the effect—the weaker level—is a form or unfolding of the stronger level. In other words, the effect must be an image of its cause and a shadow that follows it in existence. — ط
That is, every caused thing that has a nature, as discussed in The Book of Contemplations. — س ره

The “mixture” with darkness is judged with help from the imagination. Strictly speaking, darkness is the absence of light; it is not mixed with light. In any case, the account given by this discerning mystic is subtle, clear, and healing. May God guide us to the right path. — س ره

Perhaps the point is to understand the difference between the two kinds of composition. The differences between the two senses of possibility have already been discussed. The author often writes this way; the point is clear enough. — س ره

That is, whether the thing exists or does not exist absolutely, as in a simple existential judgment, or exists or does not exist under a condition, as in a predicative judgment. Assenting that fire exists causes assent that heat exists; assenting that heat does not exist causes assent that fire does not exist. Merely conceiving fire or heat does not do this, since a nature remains what it is whether considered existent or nonexistent. The same applies when assenting that the world changes leads to assent that it came into being. Al-Dawani’s objection therefore misses the point. Mental existence of a simple idea does not by itself cause assent to absolute or conditional existence or nonexistence, just as it does not do so in false judgments generally. — س ره

That is, the first principles include the truth that affirmation and denial cannot both be true and cannot both be false. Ibn Sina says something similar in The Healing, in a chapter on truth and the defense of first principles: “The first of all true statements, to which every analysis leads, is the principle that there is no middle ground between affirmation and denial.” — س ره

That is, the kind of dependence in which both the thing that depends and what it depends on belong to the same realm of meaning or nature. The phrase “especially a definition” is therefore well chosen. — س ره

As he often says, he follows the philosophers’ approach in the starting points, then parts ways with them in the conclusions. They limit growth and decline in intensity to qualities, and increase and decrease to quantities. This will be explained later, God willing. — س ره
The argument also implies that blackness would be made up of parts, even though accidents are simple things in the world outside the mind. — س ره
This means that matter may move through substantial forms, even if a nature itself cannot move in existence. — س ره

Someone might object that a void follows only when a thing that can occupy a place is missing from that place, not when a place is missing from a thing. The author does not say that a void follows if a moving thing has no place; he says it follows if the thing has no “where”—a state of the thing that involves a relation to a place. So the argument stands. That is, those imagined instants have no extension or parts. If they did, they would set the measure of motion, and motion would then occur within motion. — س ره
The more precise reading may be “instances,” as in the phrase “one temporal instance” that follows. — س ره

That is, an instance that exists in reality, not merely a nature or idea. Some thinkers say that motion, taken as a whole, is identical with this one connected temporal instance. This is supported by a later explanation: motion is a thing’s continual renewal, but renewal itself is not a separate thing; it is a relation. What exists is the category in which the renewal takes place. This is like the view that a thing’s existence is its being or coming to be: neither is a separate thing, and neither can be divided in the usual way. — س ره

The temporal instance is actual in the way temporal things are: it is neither pure possibility nor complete actuality, like something unchanging. As long as the process continues without a pause, it is one temporal instance, and its continuity gives it the unity of one thing. Al-Dawani’s account of the intermediate state could be understood this way. The author does not read him that way because he thinks al-Dawani means the moving subject never takes on any instance of the category during motion. That was not his meaning: by the intermediate state, he meant an instance that is neither pure possibility nor complete actuality, like motion itself. The “instances” here are the momentary points and temporal parts imagined as divisions, as the author explains. — س ره
This refers to the author’s argument that existence itself does not move, and that the moving thing would not remain actual if existence did move. — س ره

This question was first raised in logic, in discussions of universals and particulars. A universal may be univocal, applying in the same way to all its instances, or gradable, applying with differences of degree. Since universality is treated as a feature of essence, the discussion of gradation began with essences: philosophers had observed that things in the world differ in intensity and degree. Later, relying on Avicenna’s argument, they said that essential concepts do not vary by degree, only accidental ones. Their reasoning was that an accident has no real counterpart by itself: what exists is the subject and its accident. A derived term such as “black,” formed from blackness as it exists in a body, does not have a separate counterpart in reality, so it can vary. The difference between an accident and a derived accidental term is difficult to grasp, even though neither concept changes in meaning. On this basis, they said that two distinct essences differ either in their whole nature, in part of it, or through something outside it. The author broadens the account to include differences in existence or in thought, so it can also include degrees of existence. — ط
The fourth kind is so subtle and important that I doubt you noticed it. Yet it is a sound and solid view. — س ره

By continuing with “rather,” the author points to another flaw: the Aristotle’s followers deny the link that their argument assumes. Even if the more complete instance contains something the less complete one does not, it does not follow that the two share nothing essential. What distinguishes them may be the very feature they share, as happens with existence. — س ره

This is another Illuminationist argument against the Aristotle’s followers. If two instances of blackness differed through defining features, and a defining feature were outside the essence of the broader kind, then their difference would lie beyond blackness. But we experience the difference as a difference in blackness itself. The Illuminationists conclude that the two instances differ in themselves, not through a defining feature. — س ره
The universal nature of blackness itself does not vary; the difference is said to lie at the level of the individual.

Do not take this to mean that the concept or essence of blackness itself varies. Here “blackness” means the reality of an individual instance: broader kind and defining feature come together only in the individual. — ن ره
This is only an appeal to what seems implausible; it is not a sound basis for deciding what is true. — ط
The author attributes this argument in al-Taqdīsāt to earlier philosophers, including Avicenna in The Healing and others of his school. — س ره

The argument is quoted from Avicenna, but the author’s reply does not work. Gradation—difference within sameness—requires one thing to be predicated of another while some of its instances are excluded from others under that same predication. If gradation occurred at the level of essence, where only basic definitional predication applies, there would have to be at least two concepts, each predicated of the other in that basic way and excluded from it in the same way. A fixed concept cannot support this. — ط

As the later discussions of knowledge, power, will, good, and purpose will show, there is another kind of difference between two things. It does not fit the rule for gradation given here, nor any of the three kinds of difference listed at the start of the chapter: difference in the whole essence, in part of it, or through something outside it. Knowledge and power, for example, differ, yet each is identified with existence itself. The same is true of other realities called “existential attributes.” Their difference is not a matter of one having more than the other: knowledge is not greater than power. Nor do they differ as two essences, since they are not separate kinds of essence. But the truth is that the broader idea of difference within one reality—where what distinguishes its instances is also what they share—covers more than the rule stated here. Not every difference within a thing’s own reality, without anything added to it, is a difference that can be expressed as “more” or “less.” The philosophers should have discussed this kind of gradation separately, as they did mental and external existence, possibility and necessity, and potentiality and actuality.

The familiar kind of gradation, by degrees of excellence, requires two simple instances of one reality: the stronger includes all the perfection of the weaker and something more, while the weaker does not include all the stronger has. The weaker is intrinsically related to the stronger, though this is not a relation in the technical category of relation. The mind also sees the weaker as lacking the perfection found in the stronger, even though existence itself excludes nonexistence. This comparison is between two levels at a time. With three levels—weak, intermediate, and strong—there are two comparisons: weak to intermediate, and intermediate to strong. The intermediate is strong relative to the weak and weak relative to the strong. Treating all three as one comparison would require one relation to hold among more than two levels, and would make the middle level contain the shared reality with no increase or decrease. That would conflict with the assumed difference between what the levels share and what distinguishes them. So calling the levels “weak,” “intermediate,” and “strong” is not entirely precise. — ط

There are two cases to consider. One is a thing changing through stronger or weaker states as it moves from one kind to another—for example, from white to yellow, or from yellow to green. This is different from a weaker green becoming a stronger green. The other case is when stronger and weaker levels exist at the same time in separate things. This second case is clearer, because the levels differ both in how we understand them and in how they exist. — س ره
Some who follow Aristotle’s school allow existence to have stronger and weaker degrees, but do not allow existence itself to grow stronger or weaker through change. — س ره

This means that the levels are made individual by their own simple identities, while sharing one reality; what distinguishes them is also what they share. This can reconcile the two views. Those who say essential features can vary by degree mean “essential” as existence, the basis of a thing’s reality. Those who deny gradation in essence but allow it in what is accidental to essence mean “essence” as what a thing is, and treat existence as something added to it. — س ره
The objector is Sayyid Dāmād, in al-Taqdīsāt. — س ره

The same explanation would not work for imagined quantities that differ in length, since they have no matter whose readiness could account for the difference—unless one denies that the imaginal world exists. — س ره

Some call this mutual opposition. In fact, each intermediate shade is a simple quality and a thing in its own right. The opposition between them is the ordinary, familiar kind; it does not require the greatest possible difference. — س ره

Here “blackness” is used in more than one way. When Aristotle’s followers say that blackness is what varies, they mean each individual blackness. When they say that blackness is not what varies, they mean the shared, general nature of blackness. Their statements about the two blacknesses, the bodies that bear stronger or weaker blackness, and the idea of “black” all point to the same view: the feature that accounts for the difference is something other than the shared nature. This fits their claim that the adjective “black” applies to bodies by degrees, while blackness itself does not. — س ره

One objection is that a single motion is continuous and has one identity. If the thing it moves through is continuous too, its parts should match the whole in kind and name. How, then, could its stages be different species? The commentator replies that the quality undergoing change is not itself continuous or divisible; continuity belongs to the motion. The usual argument against Democritus concerns parts of continuous bodies, so it does not by itself prove that the levels of a quality are one species. Another reply is that a single motion must occur in one individual thing during that motion. This does not mean the mover stays the same throughout every process: a body can move through places under a series of pulls, and water can change in quality under successive fires. The point is that what one motion occurs in must be one individual thing for that motion, not a series of different species. — س ره

The difference in kind here is not between the levels of red themselves: they are all levels through which the motion passes. Red differs from black or white because it is where the process begins or ends. This is a difference in what the quality is, not in the one connected motion. — س ره

The original meaning of “strong” as the power to resist can apply to substances as well as to qualities: one thing can be more able to resist than another. This does not conflict with the technical point in the argument. It conflicts only with the wider meaning of “stronger” in everyday speech. — س ره

This refers to length itself, a kind of quantity, and to size, a feature of quantity. The author uses this to show that people do say one line is longer than another. He is not saying that measured quantity is strong in exactly the same sense as a quality; “longer” and “bigger” can simply mean “greater in amount.” — س ره
Some copies read “length is the line itself.” — ط

The distinction assumes what it is trying to prove. Strength and increase have the same basic meaning: strength that stops at a limit is increase with a limit, while increase without a limit is strength. So this does not separate them. — س ره
Both strength and increase can be divided again into forms that have a limit and forms that do not. This is a second division, made after the first division into stronger and weaker. — س ره

The examples are being compared in different ways. Five differs in kind from a smaller number such as four, and so differs in its existence as well. But one five differs in existence, not in kind, from another five. Adding five and four gives nine; adding two equal fives gives ten. With length, by contrast, a longer and a shorter measure share the same nature even though their individual extents differ. Another reading is possible: the “equal” part means the amount that matches after the extra part has been added. — س ره
That is, the shared broader kind exists in the world as a real thing; “and its existence” explains what is meant by this. — ن ره
This disproves the claim that anything that allows degrees of priority or strength must have an opposite. Existence has no opposite, yet it can be deficient, complete, or even beyond complete. — س ره

This also answers the claim that anything that admits priority or strength must undergo a process of growing stronger. Existence is a counterexample: its essence does not move or change in this way, as explained earlier. — س ره

For Aristotle’s followers, sensation is something that happens to the animal; for the author, it is an action. Movement is an action for both sides. In either case, these are features that happen to a thing; a substance is not made up of them. — س ره

Unless we rule out the possibility that effects vary because of different organs, tools, obstacles, or conditions, the objector will not agree that those effects come from the powers themselves. We must show that they do. If the tools include powers that themselves differ in completeness, then a stronger or weaker power in the substance is established. A horse’s power to perceive, for example, is more complete than a mosquito’s, especially if the soul itself has levels of development. If the difference came only from a missing condition or an obstacle, the difference between a horse’s soul and a mosquito’s would have to be permanent. That would mean the power is blocked forever, like saying that an ant can understand general ideas but never does so because a condition is always missing or an obstacle is always present. — س ره

The terms “what differs in” and “what makes the difference” are used here in the reverse way from the earlier discussion of degrees. There, the feature that causes the difference was called “what makes the difference,” and the thing that varies was “what differs in.” In discussions of priority, the feature that varies is called “what differs in.” The author is following that usage here. — س ره
The word bi-ḥayth (“such that”) appears to be a copyist’s error. The correct reading is bi-ḥasab mā (“according to what …”).

Aristotle’s followers can reply that differences in time belong to existence, not to time’s essence. This does not conflict with their claim that time itself is always passing, since “essence” here can mean either existence or the idea of time, which includes passing and is only a concept in the mind. They can also say that existences differ as separate realities, not by degrees, just as the most general kinds differ. But there is a problem: the author understands their claim about different existences as a difference attached to natures, because they are careful thinkers. If they instead mean that the existences themselves are entirely separate realities, then a single idea would have to be drawn from realities that share nothing. That would revive Ibn Kammunah’s objection and remove the shared ground between cause and effect, among other problems. — س ره

The note first states the general rule for things that overlap, then applies it to matter and form. Taken as broader kind and defining feature, they overlap as parts of one essence. Taken as matter and form, they differ, but their priority and posteriority belong to existence. — س ره
